Three things sprung out at me from this patronising op-ed by a film critic.

First, he's running mutually inconsistent arguments. On one hand he says that "if you disagree with a film critic, that's okay, he's just like one of your friends -- a guy with a particular opinion about a film, his word doesn't mean anything more than yours." On the other hand he is saying "Film critics are professionals because they see vastly more films per year than you and they're far more conversant with the language of film than you" -- implying that the critic's opinion is valuable and has more status than the average moviegoer who "only sees films 3-4 times per year, and who may not be (read: isn't) conversant with film language". You can't have it both ways: either film critics are people whose expertise makes them worth listening to or they're just another joe schmoe whose opinion is like an asshole: i.e. everybody has one.

Second: the writer makes a Freudian slip -- one that I'll expand on in a minute -- when he says "You might understandably feel angry when your opinion of the film does not match that of the vast critical/moviegoing public."

Have a think about that statement for a minute. Focus on the fact the guy runs over the assertion as if it's a given.

About the only scenario in which it's understandable that you get angry when your view of the film is different from anyone else is when you have shit-poor self-esteem or have fallen right into narcissism. Rage is the defence mechanism of anyone whose self-constructed identity becomes threatened with exposure, i.e. when someone suffers a narcissistic injury, i.e.e. you realise you might just be a weirdo who likes tights rather than the identity you've constructed for yourself as an erudite consumer of film who has a deep understanding of film (as a lot of filmgoers think they do thanks to Professor Google and Associate Professor Wiki).

But as I said I regard it as a Freudian slip, because what that remark really amounts to is projection (no pun intended). A 3-4-times-per-year cinemagoer doesn't have any vested interest or particular reason to agree with the critics. He doesn't have the knowledge or background in film to know better, for a start.

But someone who holds himself out as a film critic, as this youtuber does? That's another story. If you have a different professional view to the vast majority of professionals in your industry, it takes a lot of internal fortitude -- or narcissism -- to say "The majority of my colleagues are wrong. I'm right." Because you don't have the excuse of ignorance. Having a differing opinion in these circumstances is far more likely to cause a narcissistic injury to you, since your identity is wrapped around being an erudite, professional movie critic.

Which brings me to the third point, relating to the scoffing that the film critic community is not out to destroy audience enjoyment of films. I think this is a dreadfully naive understanding of how communities, particularly professional communities, operate. Even in supposedly "pure" disciplines like science or physics, paradigms exist, group norms exist, and people who think outside the mould are frequently sidelined or put to a much higher standard of proof than supposed scientific objectivity would dictate. How does anyone expect a subjective field like film criticism to operate differently? It may not be deliberate, but it still amounts to the same thing as academic conspiracy: a clique of "educated" and "objective" people thinking alike not because they're any smarter but because they're all wearing black-tinted glasses and therefore come to the same views. And when they see each other holding similar opinions, it reinforces the group norm.

Let's remember film critics have similar educations. They went to the same or similar schools, and they were taught with fundamentally the same assumptions and paradigms. Those paradigms are, in a nutshell, postmodernism and secular humanism - two of the most destructive academic forces we have ever entertained in the West and part of the reason people don't take Liberal Arts degrees seriously anymore.

The fact that moviegoing audiences' views are out of whack with those of the critic population all but evidences this fact. And it's got nothing to do with "anti-intellectualism" in audiences, it has everything to do with the fact the intellectuals are running on a program which is not credible or meaningful to the majority of people in the real world. Like it or not, popular opinion has much to do with a film's success because it indicates it connects with a vast swathe -- some might say a representative swathe -- of the people on planet Earth. The form of that connection -- whether because a film touches on our common biases or our common hopes -- differs, but it doesn't make a film critic any smarter because they reject that program: it just means the critic is just running a different (and in most cases inferior, incompatible) operating system.
